faq.q: Is a tsunami a tidal wave?
faq.a: People sometimes call it a tidal wave, but it has nothing to do with tides. Scientists say tsunami, because it is caused by the seabed moving, usually in an earthquake.

faq.q: Why is a tsunami so destructive?
faq.a: A tsunami moves the whole depth of the ocean and has a very long wavelength, so a huge mass of water keeps flooding inland for many minutes, carrying debris that smashes buildings.
asks: Why do tsunamis go so far inland?

faq.q: How far apart are tsunami waves?
faq.a: Tsunami crests can be over 100 kilometres apart and arrive every 10 minutes to an hour, so danger can last for hours. The first wave is often not the largest.
asks: Is the first tsunami wave the biggest?

faq.a: No. A tsunami is not a curling wave but a fast, rising surge of water full of debris that keeps coming for minutes. Anyone near the coast should move to high ground.
asks: Is a tsunami like a big wave?

faq.q: How do we get tsunami warnings?
faq.a: Seismometers detect big earthquakes within minutes, and deep-sea pressure sensors called DART buoys detect a passing tsunami. Warning centres then alert coasts that could be hit.

facts: Tsunami wavelengths can be more than 100 kilometres, while wind waves are usually well under a kilometre.
The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center was set up in Hawaii in 1949.
